To achieve your goal you have to capture the output of SHOW STREAMS https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/show-streams.html. You can start building a stored procedure that runs it and returns its output as a resultset using TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())) similar to the following one, which could be enriched by a parameter for the time window you want to check (your "1 day left) and a subsequent CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM.

Please note this is not a full solution to your problem but only half of it as it does not include the action required to re-create the stale streams.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_show_stream_stale() 
RETURNS VARIANT NOT NULL 
LANGUAGE Javascript  
EXECUTE AS Caller 
AS 
$$ 
var sql_command0 = snowflake.createStatement({ sqlText:`show streams in database`});

var sql_command1 = snowflake.createStatement({ sqlText:`SELECT "created_on"
                                                            , "name"
                                                            , "database_name"
                                                            , "schema_name"
                                                            , "owner"
                                                            , "comment"
                                                            , "table_name"
                                                            , "type"
                                                            , "stale"
                                                            , "mode"
                                                            , "stale_after" 
                                                        FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID()))`});

try { 
    sql_command0.execute();
    var db = sql_command1.execute(); 
    var json_rows = {}; 
    var array_of_rows = []; 
    var COLUMNS = ["created_on","name","database_name","schema_name","owner", "comment", "table_name", "type", "stale", "mode", "stale_after"]; 
    var row_num = 1;
    while (db.next()) {  
        json_rows = {}; 
        for (var col_num = 0; col_num < COLUMNS.length; col_num = col_num + 1) { 
            var col_name = COLUMNS[col_num]; 
            json_rows[col_name] = db.getColumnValue(col_num + 1);
        } 
        array_of_rows.push(json_rows); 
        ++row_num; 
    }
    return array_of_rows; 
}
catch (err) { 
    return "Failed: " + err;
}
$$;

As the resultset is a single JSON, you can run the stored procedure and soon after the following SELECT statement to get the resultset in tabular format.

  CALL sp_show_stream_stale();

  SELECT value:created_on::datetime as "created_on",
    value:name::string as "name",
    value:database_name::string  as "database_name",
    value:schema_name::string as "schema_name",
    value:owner::string as "owner",
    value:comment::string as "comment",
    value:table_name::string as "table_name",
    value:type::string as "type",
    value:stale::string as "stale",
    value:mode::string as "mode",
    value:stale_after::datetime as "stale_after"
  FROM (SELECT * FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())))
      , LATERAL FLATTEN(Input => sp_show_stream_stale)    
  WHERE DATEDIFF(Day, current_timestamp, value:stale_after::datetime) <= 1 ;

just use one SELECT statement and use a CASE statement to calculate Is_Latest_Quarter

UPDATED WITH (ALMOST) ACTUAL SQL

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE VIEW VIEW_NAME AS
SELECT {list of columns you want to include}
,CASE WHEN snapshot_dt=(select max(snapshot_dt) from base_tbl) THEN 1 
 ELSE 0 END as Is_Latest_Quarter
FROM base_tbl 
full outer JOIN lkp_tbl on base_tbl.CUST_ID = lkp_tbl.CUST_ID

Alternatively, if Snowflake doesn't like that in-line subquery, your could use a CTE something like:

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE VIEW VIEW_NAME AS
    WITH MAX_DATE AS (SELECT MAX(Ssnapshot_dt) AS max_snapshot_dt FROM base_tbl),
    SELECT {list of columns you want to include}
    ,CASE WHEN max_date.max_snapshot_dt is not null  THEN 1 
     ELSE 0 END as Is_Latest_Quarter
    FROM base_tbl 
    full outer JOIN lkp_tbl on base_tbl.CUST_ID = lkp_tbl.CUST_ID
    LEFT OUTER JOIN MAX_DATE ON base_tbl.snapshot_dt = max_date.max_snapshot_dt

Brief description could be found in the following document: The Snowflake Elastic Data Warehouse by Snowflake Computing

3.3.1 Query Management and Optimization

(...)

Snowflake’s query optimizer follows a typical Cascades- style approach [28], with top-down cost-based optimization. All statistics used for optimization are automatically main- tained on data load and updates. Since Snowflake does not use indices (cf. Section 3.3.3), the plan search space is smaller than in some other systems. The plan space is further reduced by postponing many decisions until execu- tion time, for example the type of data distribution for joins. This design reduces the number of bad decisions made by the optimizer, increasing robustness at the cost of a small loss in peak performance. It also makes the system easier to use (performance becomes more predictable), which is in line with Snowflake’s overall focus on service experience. Once the optimizer completes, the resulting execution plan is distributed to all the worker nodes that are part of the query. As the query executes, Cloud Services continuously tracks the state of the query to collect performance counters and detect node failures. All query information and statis- tics are stored for audits and performance analysis. (...)

I find "knowing the 'rules'" less helpful, than understanding what the system is doing as more helpful.

I have found describing it to new team members has massive table scans, that do map/reduce/merge joins.

You can make the tables scans faster by selecting the smallest set of columns needed to get the answer you need.

There is partition pruning so if you have data in a 'inserted/sorted' order of x 1-2,3-4,5-6 and your query has x = 5, then the first two partitions will not be read.

Next because it's all merge joins, equi joins are the fastest thing todo. [Edit:] This is trying to say, that at the order of million's of rows and up. Joining 1m rows to 1m rows based on complex join logic like a.v1 > b.v2 or a.v2 < b.v3 ... etc means you have to more or less make you trillion+ rows and just try and see. Where-as if you can join on exact values a.v1 = b.v2 and a.v2 = b.v2 now the data can be sorted with respect to those keys, and a merge join can be done, and your performance is very good (sort-merge join on Wikipedia).

This means sometimes reading from the same set of source tables many times in different CTE's and joining those can be the fastest way to process large volumes of data. [Edit:] which in the context of the above statement often in small db SQL people do correlated sub-queries, because a) you can, so why not, and b) they can be fast on indexed databases. But in snowflake with no indexes, besides the optimizer doesn't support most correlated sub-queries, you generally should avoid them and read the data twice in two CTEs and join/left-join those via a equi-join to answer the question that is done, as the CTE's tasks are independent, thus parallelisable, and the merge-join is near-optimal. And the waste of calculating (lets pretend sub-totals) for data that is not in the main join body, is less that gains of parallelism. (this holds best for queries in the 30 seconds or longer range, as compared to speeding up sub 5 second sized queries). But with everything, have a base model, and try/experiment, and poke and the slow stuff, till you cannot restructure you data or query to make it faster.

As always look at the profile of the run query, and look for area there many rows are dropped, and think how you can restructure the logic to push these restrictions earlier in the pipeline.

Query Optimization:

Snowflake supports query vectorization and does some cost-based optimization. But its first-time run of queries are typically seconds-to-minutes. Snowflake has added local disk “caching” and also a result cache to speed up subsequent queries for repetitive workloads like reporting and dashboards.

Optimized Storage:

Snowflake has a micro-partition file system that is more optimized than S3 and supports partitioning and sorting with cluster keys Split the data into multiple small files to support optimal data loading in Snowflake.

IMPROVING QUERY PERFORMANCE

  1. Consider implementing clustering keys for large tables.
  2. Try to execute relatively homogeneous queries (size, complexity, data sets, etc.) on the same warehouse.

IMPROVING LOAD PERFORMANCE

  1. Use bulk loading to get the data into tables in Snowflake. Consider splitting large data files so the load can be efficiently distributed across servers in a cluster.
  2. Delete from internal stages files that are no longer needed. You may notice an improvement performance in addition to saving on costs.
  3. Isolate load and transform jobs from queries to prevent resource contention. Dedicate separate warehouses for loading and querying operations to optimize performance for each.
  4. Leverage the scalable compute layer to do the bulk of the data processing. Consider using Snowpipe in micro-batching scenarios. Your query may benefit from cached results from a previous execution.
  5. Use separate warehouses for your queries and load tasks. This will facilitate targeted provisioning of warehouses and avoid any resource contention between dissimilar operations.
  6. Use a separate data warehouse for large files.
    The number and capacity of the servers determine the number of data files.

Segment Data

Snowflake caches data in the virtual data warehouse, but it's still essential to segment data. Consider these best practices for data query performance:

Group users with common queries in the same virtual data warehouse to optimize data retrieval and use.

Scale-Up

Snowflake supports fast and easy adjustments to the warehouse-size to handle the workload.
It can also automatically suspend or resume the scale-up, with complete transparency for the user.
Snowflake's scale-up functionality supports the continually changing requirements for processing.

Scale-Out

Snowflake supports the deployment of same-size clusters to support concurrency. Keep these points in mind for how scale-out can help performance optimization:

As users execute queries, the virtual data warehouse automatically adds clusters up to a fixed limit.
It can scale-up in a more controlled way instead of deploying one or more clusters of larger machines like legacy data platforms.

I found the best way to switch to PyQt and back to inline is through the 'close_event' in mpl_connect. Here is an outline of what I did:

def function(foo):
    #Switches to qt interactive backend
    %matplotlib qt
    ...
    fig = plt.figure(...)
    ...
    def on_close(event):
        %matplotlib inline
    fig.canvas.mpl_connect('close_event', on_close) #Switches backend to inline when the figure closes
    ...
    return None

It works perfectly on my Windows machine. I can close the figure window using the default close button, or by passing plt.close() using a Matplotlib widget. The backend switches back to inline in both cases.

Another way of doing this in a non-global way is using the matplotlib.pyplot.rc_context context manager, as follows:

with plt.rc_context({
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
}):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ...

In case you want to apply this on a frequent basis, you can also create a style sheet as described here and use these settings yourstyle.mplstyle:

axes.spines.left:   True
axes.spines.bottom: True
axes.spines.top:    False
axes.spines.right:  False

You then import it:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use('./yourfolder/yourstyle.mplstyle')

It is possible to derive such a style from tidyverse_style. (As stated in earlier answer) Below example is the minimal needed code, which is only about 20 lines give and take. This code example was copied from here. Modifying styler one rule can have some idiosyncratic side-effects, which needs a bit more code to handle. But with a little fiddling it can work out fine.

rpolars_style = function() {
  # derive from tidyverse
  transformers = styler::tidyverse_style()
  transformers$style_guide_name = "rpolars_style"
  transformers$style_guide_version = "0.1.1"

  # reverse tranformer to make <- into =
  transformers$token$force_assignment_op = function(pd) {
    to_replace = pd$token == "LEFT_ASSIGN"

    # pretect against changing globalAssign operator, which does not have a unique defined token.
    if (any(to_replace)) {
      to_replace = to_replace & pd$text != "<<-"
    }

    pd$token[to_replace] = "EQ_ASSIGN"
    pd$text[to_replace] = "="
    pd
  }

  # Specify which tokens must be absent for a transformer to be dropped
  # https://styler.r-lib.org/reference/specify_transformers_drop.html?q=transformers%20_%20drop
  transformers$transformers_drop$token$force_assignment_op = "LEFT_ASSIGN"

  transformers
}

#use example
styler::style_dir(path = ".", style = rpolars_style())

If you want to use an operation in broadcast, among batch_pattern and multiple clusters, here's a possible solution:

diff = (batch_pattern - mean_n_cluster).unsqueeze(2) 
left_term = torch.einsum('bcik,cki->bci',diff,inv_cov_n_cluster) 
under_radix = torch.einsum('bci,bci->bc',left_term,diff.squeeze(2))
mahalanobis_dist = torch.sqrt(under_radix)

where
batch_pattern (batch_size x 1 x n_features) is the input tensor representing the batch of points
mean_n_cluster (n_cluster x n_features) is the tensor representing the mean of the cluster
inv_cov_n_cluster (n_cluster x n_features x n_features) is the tensor representing the inverse of the covariance matrix

You can simply change plt.xscale('symlog') to plt.xscale('log'). 'symlog' is an extension of the 'log' scale for negative values, which you do not need here. Naturally, this extension is not seamless, and it needs to remove values under a small threshhold. That is what is causing you issues here.

Be careful because if you need to plot for values starting at 0.1, you need to change t at the beginning.

Full code:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.logspace(-1, 4, 100)

CP = 400
P_an = 1100
tau = 30

P = CP+P_an/(1+t/tau)

As MrXerios pointed out, the plotting artifacts were due to applying symmetrical logarithimic scaling to x, i.e., plt.xscale('symlog').

After reading up on the documentation, I realized that 'symlog' applies linear scaling to a near-zero range, to avoid values going to infinity. This range is defined by the attribute linthresh, which is set to equal 2 by default (i.e., the scaling is linear for [-2, 2]).

Therefore, there is a solution to the problem by keeping symlog and including linthresh=1, as the minimum value on the x-axis was one in this example.

plt.xscale('symlog', linthresh=1)

mu = exact centre dot (1D).
L = Stretched shape of the entire cloud. May be 2D. Shape = [Dim,Dim]. It has both rows and columns.
We have to Transpose it, L.T to trick the F.linear
b = If you take a single point on a graph and stretch it using a grid(L).
The result will be a A new point(1D) somewhere else on the graph.
1D tensor cannot transposed. Therefore, b.T is mathematically meaningless and not needed.
L = torch.linalg.cholesky(precision)
b = -(mu @ L)
While using F.linear(Data, Weights), it transposes or flips the Weights matrix
before it does the multiplication. So no matter what you give, F.linear = Data * Weights^T
So here, I will use W = L^T .
Now, Feed this : F.linear(Z,W)
=> machine computes Z @ W^T + b
=> Z @ (L^T)^T + b
=> Z @ L + b

Then Use Contiguous.
Calling .contiguous() in _init_ is like Chopping all the vegetables and everything else
and putting them in organized containers before a restaurant opens.




import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class ProductionMahalanobis(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, mu: torch.Tensor, precision: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        dim = precision.size(-1)
        eye = torch.eye(dim, dtype = precision.dtype, device = precision.device)
        safe_precision = precision * (eye * jitter)
        # 1. MATH
        L = torch.linalg.cholesky(safe_precision)          
        b = -(mu @ L)                                 
        
        # 2. Using .contiguous() as safeguard
        # F.linear physically executes as (Z @ W.T). 
        # Because we want Z @ L, we must store W = L.T. 
        # .contiguous() pays the memory-copy penalty offline so inference is instant.
        self.register_buffer("W", L.T.contiguous())   
        self.register_buffer("b", b.contiguous())     
        self.eps = eps

    @torch.inference_mode()
    def forward(self, Z: torch.Tensor, squared : bool = False) -> torch.Tensor:
        
        # Using F.linear, PyTorch treats this statistical formula as a standard 
        # Deep Learning layer, making it the absolute fastest cuBLAS execution path.
        y = F.linear(Z, self.W, self.b)    
                   
        
        d2 = (y * y).sum(dim = -1)

        # if squared = True then we are doing just a True/False check. Hence no need for square root.
        # if squared =False gives Exact Distance. this works for all   those who want to work with
        # the standard deviations. 

        if squared : return d2
        return d2.clamp_min(self.eps).sqrt()

I'm the author of curved-text, a small package I wrote for labeling curves directly in plots. It works for this case of road names too. You can install it with pip install curved-text.

Here is a version of the road case from the question.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from curved_text import curved_text

# A curved road as an ordered sequence of (x, y) points
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
x = 10 * t
y = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(x, y, color="0.4", linewidth=18, solid_capstyle="round")
curved_text(ax, x, y, "Riverside Drive", pos=0.3, anchor="center",
            color="white", fontsize=13)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.margins(0.08)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()

Image result with curved text along a road

The positioning of the label is controlled with three parameters:

  • pos is the position along the road, as a fraction of its length.
  • anchor is the part of the label that sits at pos ("start", "center", or "end").
  • offset moves the label sideways off the line, in points. For this road, offset=20 puts the name beside the road.

The points need to be in order along the road. I think road data from a file such as OpenStreetMap XML is usually in that order already. The layout is redone every time the figure is drawn, so the label stays on the road when you resize, pan, or zoom.

For plain text, curved-text also places one character at a time, like the accepted answer, but there are a few differences.

  • Baselines. The accepted answer makes each character a rotated Text. Matplotlib aligns a rotated Text by its rotated bounding box, which has a different shape for each glyph, so the characters' baselines move a little relative to each other. I measured this on a straight line with 24 pt text at 200 dpi. The baselines were spread over 1.5 to 3 pixels at angles from 20 to 60 degrees, and there was no spread on a horizontal line. curved-text draws each character from its glyph outline and puts all of them on one shared baseline, and in the same test the baseline spread was under 0.2 pixels.
  • Spaces. The accepted answer draws each space as an invisible "a". In the default font an "a" is almost twice as wide as a space, so the gaps between words come out wider than normal. curved-text draws spaces as spaces.
  • End of the curve. In the accepted answer, characters that run past the end of the curve are hidden. curved-text extends the curve in a straight line from its last direction and puts the extra characters there.
  • Math. In the accepted answer, a $...$ run is split into separate characters. curved-text typesets it as math and bends it along the curve, and it also supports usetex=True.

The documentation and more examples are at https://thiebes.github.io/curved-text/. If you try it and something doesn't work, please open an issue on GitHub. I'd be glad to hear about it.

This was a known limitation of Snowflake session variables. When using multi-variable assignment:

SET (var1, var2) = (
  SELECT col1, col2
);

Snowflake enforced a 256-byte limit on string/binary session variables, so your Unicode string exceeds the limit even though the character count looks small. The error message is reporting the internal byte size (280 bytes in your example), not the number of characters.

I don't think it's related to tuple/array storage. It's just the session variable size restriction that applied to this form of SET assignment. Snowflake later increased the limit to 16 KB, so the same example works on current releases.

Before changing the SQL, check the Query Profile. In most cases the bottleneck is either large table scans, data skew, excessive joins, or poor pruning.

A few things that usually help:

  • Filter data as early as possible.

  • Avoid SELECT *.

  • Ensure clustering keys match common filter predicates.

  • Reduce unnecessary joins/subqueries.

  • Check if the warehouse is spending time on compute or I/O before simply scaling it up.

The Query Profile will usually tell you where the actual bottleneck is.

I'd start with the Query Profile. In Snowflake, join performance issues are often caused by large table scans rather than the join operation itself.

Things I'd check:

  • Are filters being applied before the join?

  • Is partition pruning happening on both tables?

  • Are you joining on expressions/functions instead of raw columns?

  • Is one table small enough to be broadcast efficiently?

Also, if the same query is run frequently, consider clustering on the commonly used join/filter columns. In my experience, reducing the amount of data scanned usually gives a bigger improvement than trying to optimize the join syntax itself.

Views themselves are usually not the performance problem. Snowflake expands the view definition at runtime, so performance depends on the underlying query, joins, filters, and amount of data being scanned.

I'd check the Query Profile first. If the view contains multiple nested views, complex joins, or prevents partition pruning, that can have a noticeable impact. In many cases, simplifying the view logic or querying the base tables directly helps identify the real bottleneck.

Clustering only helps when your query filters align with the clustering key and Snowflake can prune micro-partitions effectively.

If performance is still poor on a clustered table, I'd check:

  • Whether the query predicates match the clustering key.

  • The table's clustering depth (SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION).

  • How many micro-partitions are being scanned in the Query Profile.

  • Whether joins or aggregations, rather than the table scan itself, are the real bottleneck.

I've seen cases where a well-clustered table still performs poorly because the query is scanning most of the table, leaving little opportunity for partition pruning.

Your clustering looks healthy (average_depth = 1 and almost all partitions are constant), so the issue is probably not partition pruning.

For a delete of ~1/25th of a 520B-row table, Snowflake still has to rewrite metadata and maintain table history, which can be expensive. Since you're removing an entire month, I'd check how many rows match 'Mar 2019' and whether the cloning environment has enough warehouse capacity.

If this is a recurring process, consider storing each month separately (or using a partition-switching style approach) rather than doing large monthly deletes. In my experience, large-scale deletes on multi-terabyte tables are often slower than expected even when clustering is optimal.

A solution using the base R function splinefun() to generate a smoothed edge (spline).

Note that both brazil and distribution are multipolygon sf. This is somewhat fortuitous as it required some extra processing, and is likely to be more representative of a 'real world' scenario.

As such, this solution uses subsetting to manage the presence of multipolygon features. For example, to simplify the process, only the polygon from distribution that needs splining (e.g. not the small islands) and the corresponding brazil polygon are used. You can skip the polygon subsetting if your real data have a one-to-one relationship.

The following could be condensed further, but I expect the parameters used below may not be suitable in every case. Leaving it verbose should make it easier to intercept and correct any issues that may arise.

The workflow:

  1. Extract coast-only edges from distribution polygon as a line sf
  2. Extract non-coast distribution vertices
  3. Get start and end vertices of coast line sf from step 1 and combine with non-coast distribution vertices from previous step. This will ensure the resulting spline starts and ends at the coast-only edges
  4. Derive matrix of coordinates from previous step, calculate cumulative distance between coordinates, and generate finer resolution vector of distances for smoother result
  5. Create custom splinefun() functions anchored to coordinates matrix from previous step
  6. Apply functions from previous step to distances vector from step 4 to derive splined coordinates
  7. Use coordinates from previous step to generate splined line sf, join result to coast line sf, convert to polygon, add result to subsetted distribution sf

You can safely ignore all the warnings returned by this code.

Create example data:

library(sf)
library(lwgeom)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Load coast example, st_cast() to individual polygons
brazil <- ne_countries(country = "Brazil", scale = "medium") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  select() # Drop all columns except geometry

occurrences <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(X = c(-50, -52, -48, -42, -43),
             Y = c(-28, -20, -15, -18, -23)),
  coords = c("X","Y"),
  crs = 4326)

# Create example polygon, st_cast() to individual polygons as with brazil
# If real distribution sf contains attribute columns, make backup
# and run select() as above
distribution <- st_sf(
  geometry = st_convex_hull(st_union(occurrences))
  ) |> 
  st_intersection(brazil) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON")

Create point sf, the basis for spline:

# Set buffer in decimal degrees (to account for floating point issues)
# Using buffers may not be required for projected data
buff <- 0.000001

# Return coast-only part of distribution polygon
# If target polygons !max(area), replace slice_max() with indices
# of target polygons e.g. distribution[1,] or equivalent
coast <- st_intersection(
  st_buffer(
    st_boundary(
      brazil |> slice_max(st_area(geometry), n = 1)
      # brazil[1,]
    ),
    buff,
    endCapStyle = "FLAT"
  ),
  st_boundary(
    distribution |> slice_max(st_area(geometry), n = 1)
    # distribution[1,]
  )
)

# Return non-coast vertices from distribution polygon
# and add id for validating point order
pt <- st_difference(
  # distribution[1,] |>
  distribution |>
    slice_max(st_area(geometry), n = 1) |>
  st_cast("POINT"),
  st_buffer(coast, buff, endCapStyle = "FLAT")
  ) |>
  mutate(id = row_number() + 1)

# Return end and start point of coast
se_pt <- st_sf(
  geometry = c(st_endpoint(coast), st_startpoint(coast))
  ) |>
  mutate(id = c(1, max(pt$id + 1)))

# Combine pt and se_pt vertices in anti-clockwise direction
distrib_pt <- rbind(se_pt[1,], pt, se_pt[2,])

# Check anti-clockwise point order, redo se_pt/distrib_pt if necessary
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = distrib_pt, colour = "grey") +
  geom_sf_text(data = distrib_pt, aes(label = id))

Create splined line sf, join to coast and convert to polygon:

# Extract distrib_pt coordinates
coords <- st_coordinates(distrib_pt)

# Calculate cumulative distance between vertices
seg_dist <- sqrt(diff(coords[, "X"])^2 + diff(coords[, "Y"])^2)
cumu_dist <- c(0, cumsum(seg_dist))

# To help prevent overly exaggerated splines, and to ensure a smoother curve,
# create finer resolution distances vector e.g. * 10 more vertices
seg_dist <- seq(0, max(cumu_dist), length.out = nrow(coords) * 10)

# Create function to anchor spline to coords
# method options: "fmm", "periodic", "natural", "monoH.FC", "hyman"
spline_x <- splinefun(x = cumu_dist, y = coords[, "X"], method = "fmm")
spline_y <- splinefun(x = cumu_dist, y = coords[, "Y"], method = "fmm")

# Derive spline coordinates based on finer resolution distances vector
x_coords <- spline_x(seg_dist)
y_coords <- spline_y(seg_dist)

# Build line sf from splined coordinates, join to coast, create polygon,
# replace original distribution polygon with splined version
distrib_poly <- st_sf(
  geometry = st_sfc(
    st_linestring(cbind(x_coords, y_coords)),
    crs = st_crs(distrib_pt)
    )
  ) |>
  bind_rows(coast) |>
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry)) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  bind_rows(
    distribution |>
      arrange(desc(st_area(geometry))) |>
      slice(-1)
    # distribution[-1,]
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = brazil, colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = distrib_poly, fill = "darkred") +
  geom_sf(data = occurrences) +
  ylim(c(-30, -12)) +
  xlim(c(-60, -40)) +
  theme_minimal()

Relative to the original answer below, this result appears to be more representative of the original distribution, particularly around the southernmost area by the coast.

If you want to get a better idea of what it's doing, run splinefun to see the source code. I chose method = "fmm" as it produced the closest match to your sketch. Other method options may be a better fit in certain cases.

Snowflake uses a cost optimizer rather than a traditional rule-based optimizer (RBO). However, it also performs several automatic query rewrites and heuristic optimizations before choosing the final execution plan.

The optimizer evaluates different ways of executing a query and chooses a plan based on estimated cost, data volume, filtering, joins, aggregations, and other factors.

Unlike traditional databases where you may think primarily about indexes, Snowflake relies heavily on micro partitions

Snowflake uses a columnar architecture, so avoid , select * from table

Large joins can be expensive because Snowflake may need to redistribute data across compute nodes.

For very large tables with frequently used selective filters, clustering can improve micro-partition pruning.

Try to write snowflake queries that gives the optimizer good opportunities and then validate the result using Query Profile.

Yes, but there is an important difference between both the BI tool

In Power BI, when you use Python as a data source, Power BI can directly recognize Pandas DataFrames created by the script as tables. Tableau does not provide an equivalent mechanism where arbitrary DataFrames from a Python script automatically appear as separate tables in the Tableau data-source UI.

A single DELETE is the right tool for this, and 800k out of 5M is not a large delete for Snowflake.

What matters for cost is not the row count but how many micro-partitions the rows live in. Snowflake's storage is immutable, so DELETE rewrites every micro-partition that contains at least one matching row. If the rows you're removing are concentrated (say, one date range or one customer), only those partitions are rewritten and the statement finishes quickly. If they're scattered across the whole table, Snowflake ends up rewriting most of the table either way, and at 5M rows that is still seconds to a few minutes on a small warehouse.

A few practical steps:

  1. Count first, so you know what the predicate matches:

    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM my_table WHERE <predicate>;

  2. If the rows to delete come from another table, join to it rather than building a giant IN list:

    DELETE FROM my_table t

    USING rows_to_remove r

    WHERE t.id = r.id;

  3. Check the result before you move on. If it went wrong, Time Travel gets you back without a restore:

    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM my_table BEFORE (STATEMENT => '<query id of the delete>');

Only reach for INSERT OVERWRITE INTO my_table SELECT ... WHERE NOT <predicate> (or a CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT) when you're removing most of the table, because those rewrite everything regardless. INSERT OVERWRITE keeps the table object, grants and history; CREATE OR REPLACE gives you a new table and drops the Time Travel history unless you need that reset anyway.

One last thing people are surprised by: storage doesn't fall right away. The deleted partitions stay in Time Travel and then Fail-safe for the retention period, so the storage drop shows up after that window ends.

The problem is that since you have 6 columns of input data, bootnet keeps 6 labels of the nodes, while your custom estimator generates a 4 × 4 network. As a result, bootnet() tries to find 6 labels for 4 nodes and does not succeed. Specify the names of the four resulting nodes explicitly:

node_names <- c("src", "sex", "hmhr", "wmwr")

network1 <- estimateNetwork(
  data = data1,
  fun = impute_estimator,
  type = type_mgm,
  level = level_mgm,
  labels = node_names
)

network1$labels <- node_names
network1$nNode <- length(node_names)

Also inside impute_estimator() after creating final add-

dimnames(final) <- list(node_names, node_names)
return(final)

So .id and .imp are not the problem. The problem is simply the mismatch between the original 6 variables and the final 4 network nodes. After making the labels match the 4×4 graph bootnet() can process the network correctly.

Here is a solution matching requirements 2 and 3.

I do not understand requirement 2, so I include a function with the formula interface. It's a simple one-liner.

The second function first splits the column vectors by groups of grp, then runs the t tests on each of the sp list members.

I also test equality of the functions' results.

Note that none of the functions needs a results vector to be created beforehand, apply will take care of that. apply's return value is the vector returned by its anonymous function.

t_test_matrix_1 <- function(mat, grp) {
  apply(mat, 2, \(x) t.test(x ~ grp)$statistic)
}

t_test_matrix_2 <- function(mat, grp) {
  apply(mat, 2, \(x) {
    sp <- split(x, grp)
    if(length(sp) < 2L) {
      stop("not enough groups to run a t-test.")
    } else {
      if(any(lengths(sp) < 2)) {
        warning("both groups must have at least 2 elements, returning 'NA'.")
        NA
      } else t.test(sp[[1L]], sp[[2L]])$statistic
    }
  })
}

set.seed(2026)
n <- 200
m <- 1000
mat <- matrix(rnorm(m * n, mean = 20, sd = 3), nrow = 200)
grp <- rep(0:1, times = 100)

# Calling the function: 
t1 <- t_test_matrix_1(mat, grp)
t2 <- t_test_matrix_2(mat, grp)
identical(t1, t2)
#> [1] TRUE

# Checking to make sure the function output is a vector of length 1000:
length(t1)
#> [1] 1000
length(t2)
#> [1] 1000

Created on 2026-10-06 with reprex v2.1.1

For matrix m and group assignments g:

apply(m, 2, \(x) t.test(x[g == 1L], x[!g])$statistic)

What this does: MARGIN is 2, so it takes each column (second dimension) of m and passes it to the function defined in the FUN argument. That function subsets its argument x by the value of g and calls t.test with the two subsets. Adding $statistic to the end of t.test will cause the function to return only the test statistic.

Full demonstration:

set.seed(0)
m <- matrix(rnorm(200*1000), 200, 1000)
g <- as.integer(runif(200) < 0.5)
res <- apply(m, 2, \(x) t.test(x[g == 1L], x[!g])$statistic)
res[1:10]

To save the output from dm_draw():

  1. Convert the plot to an SVG by piping DiagrammeRsvg::export_svg() into your plot code
  2. Use rsvg::rsvg_png() to save your SVG as a PNG

Note that in this dm GitHub issue, a user stated:

I have been able to save these as svg files following your reply, but have struggled to export to png while preserving the fonts.

This comment refers to the fact that the text might 'bleed' outside the boxes (such as in the reprex you supplied). To correct this, you can examine the font parameters in the SVG file by running cat(), then modifying the font size/s using gsub() where necessary.

pak::pak("cynkra/dm")
### May need to also update
# install.packages("dplyr")
# install.packages("dbplyr")
# install.packages("DiagrammeR")

library(dplyr)
library(dm)
library(DiagrammeRsvg)
library(rsvg)

# Render plot, export to SVG
dm_svg <- dm_nycflights13() %>%
  dm_draw() %>%
  export_svg()

# Examine SVG (result omtited for the sake of brevity)
cat(dm_svg)

# Modify box headings font size
dm_svg <- gsub(
  'font-size="14.00" fill="#ffffff"',
  'font-size="12.00" fill="#ffffff"',
  dm_svg
  )

# Modify list font size
dm_svg <- gsub(
  'font-size="14.00" fill="#444444"',
  'font-size="10.00" fill="#444444"',
  dm_svg
  )

rsvg_png(
  charToRaw(dm_svg),
  "C:/test/flights_model.png",
  width = 600,
  height = 600
  )

The above image saved at 600dpi to keep file size down, 1200dpi produces a 'crisp' result.

Using the same technique used to change the font sizes, you can also tweak the other elements in the plot. If special characters exist in the SVG strings you want to change, you will need to add fixed = TRUE to your gsub().

I know this is an old question, but the problem with the code is you have already dumped the object to the pickled stream and the pickle protocol will recognize that it has already dumped the object and use a special instruction instead of re-dumping the pickled object.

This code should work (at least on Python 3.14) for two different obj instances:

import pickle, io

class MyClass:
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (MyClass, tuple())

buffer = io.BytesIO()
pickler = pickle.Pickler(buffer)

obj = MyClass()
pickler.dump(obj)

def myreduce(self):
    print("hello")
    return (MyClass, tuple())

patched = MyClass()
patched.__reduce__ = types.MethodType(myreduce, patched)
pickler.dump(patched)
